newsitem.title: USA: SOLAR STORM MAY DISRUPT SOME POWER GRIDS - NASA.
newsitem.headline: SOLAR STORM MAY DISRUPT SOME POWER GRIDS - NASA.

text.p: A large storm on the sun's surface probably will hit the earth's magnetic field later on Wednesday, with the potential to disrupt some communications satellites and some power grids, NASA said.

"It's clearly a big event," said Don Savage, a spokesman for the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's Office of Space Science. A large solar flare was blamed for the destruction of a broadcast satellite in January.

Savage said matter blown off the face of the sun -- essentially a stream of ionised particles -- was expected to strike a "glancing blow" to the magnetic field that shields the Earth more than 100 miles (160 km) from its surface.

He said those who operate sensitive satellites and power grids had already been warned to take unspecified steps to safeguard their operations through an established early-warning system that reports "space weather."

The solar storm was detected about 48 hours ago by the Solar and Heliospheric Observatory, a satellite that NASA and the European Space Agency launched in 1995 to keep a constant eye on the sun's surface.

Savage said scientists were still calculating the precise arrival time of the solar impact, which was likely to produce a shimmering curtain of multi-coloured light called an aurora over the North and South poles.
